headline: The easiest green to sneak into anything
intro: A big bag cooks down to almost nothing, so a whole handful vanishes into curries, eggs and sauces. Fresh or frozen both count.

benefits.title: Vitamin K
benefits.detail: A cup of cooked spinach has more than a day's worth. It helps your blood clot normally and supports healthy bones.

benefits.title: Folate
benefits.detail: A B vitamin your body uses to make new cells. Leafy greens are one of the best everyday sources.

benefits.title: Plant iron
benefits.detail: Spinach has iron, but the plant kind is harder to absorb. Pair it with vitamin C, like tomatoes or a squeeze of lemon, to get more of it.

choose: Look for crisp, deep-green leaves. Skip bags with wet or darkened leaves at the bottom.
store: Keep it in its bag with a paper towel to soak up moisture, and use it within about 5 days. Frozen spinach works in anything cooked.
kidTip: Blend a handful into a smoothie or pasta sauce. It disappears.

headline: Dinner in 30 minutes, no soaking
intro: Lentils cook straight from the bag, cost very little, and turn a pot of spices into a filling dinner.

benefits.title: Plant protein
benefits.detail: A cup of cooked lentils has about as much protein as three eggs.

benefits.title: Lots of fiber
benefits.detail: That same cup gives more than half a day's fiber, which keeps everyone full for longer.

benefits.title: Folate and iron
benefits.detail: Lentils are one of the richest plant sources of both.

serving.label: ¼ cup dry (about ¾ cup cooked)

choose: Red lentils cook soft in about 15 minutes, perfect for dal and soups. Brown and green ones hold their shape for salads and stews.
store: Keep dry lentils in an airtight jar for up to a year. Cooked lentils keep 4–5 days in the fridge.
kidTip: Stir cooked red lentils into bolognese or taco meat. They blend right in.

headline: Sweet, cheap and keeps for weeks
intro: Roast them, mash them or cube them into a curry. They're naturally sweet, so they're an easy sell at the table.

benefits.title: Vitamin A
benefits.detail: The orange color is beta-carotene, which your body turns into vitamin A. One medium sweet potato covers more than a day's worth.

benefits.title: Fiber
benefits.detail: Most of it is in and just under the skin, so scrub them well and leave it on.

benefits.title: Potassium
benefits.detail: A good source of this mineral, which helps muscles and nerves work.

choose: Pick firm ones with smooth skin and no soft or wrinkly spots.
store: Keep them somewhere cool and dark, not the fridge, and they'll last 2–3 weeks.
kidTip: Cut into wedges and roast until the edges caramelize. Sweet potato fries, basically.

headline: Omega-3s on the table in 20 minutes
intro: Salmon cooks fast, doesn't need much, and frozen or canned is just as good for weeknights.

benefits.title: Omega-3 fats
benefits.detail: Oily fish like salmon are one of the best sources of EPA and DHA. Dietary guidelines suggest eating seafood about twice a week.

benefits.title: Protein
benefits.detail: A 4 oz fillet has over 20 grams.

benefits.title: Vitamin D
benefits.detail: One of the few foods that naturally has a meaningful amount.

choose: Frozen fillets are usually cheaper than fresh and just as good. Canned salmon is great for patties and bowls.
store: Cook fresh salmon within 1–2 days. Thaw frozen fillets overnight in the fridge.
kidTip: A sweet glaze, like honey-garlic or teriyaki, wins over fish skeptics.

headline: The can that saves dinner
intro: Keep a few cans in the pantry and a salad, a curry or a crunchy snack is never more than 15 minutes away.

benefits.title: Fiber
benefits.detail: Half a cup gives about a fifth of a day's fiber, which helps keep energy steady.

benefits.title: Plant protein
benefits.detail: Protein and fiber together make chickpeas filling, even in a light meal.

benefits.title: Folate
benefits.detail: Beans and peas are among the best sources of this B vitamin.

choose: Go for low-sodium cans, or rinse regular ones to wash off some of the salt.
store: Move leftovers out of the can into a covered container and use them within 3–4 days.
kidTip: Pat them dry, toss with a little oil and paprika, and roast until crunchy.

headline: The green most kids will actually eat
intro: Steamed, stir-fried or roasted until the edges crisp, broccoli is the dependable weeknight vegetable.

benefits.title: Vitamin C
benefits.detail: A cup of raw broccoli has nearly a day's worth.

benefits.title: Vitamin K
benefits.detail: Broccoli is also a good source of vitamin K, which helps with normal blood clotting.

benefits.title: Fiber
benefits.detail: The stalks count too. Peel and slice them into stir-fries.

choose: Look for tight, dark-green heads with no yellowing. Frozen florets are fine for cooking.
store: Keep it unwashed in a loose bag in the crisper, and use within 3–5 days.
kidTip: Roast it until the tips crisp up, or call them "little trees".

headline: Budget protein that fills everyone up
intro: Black beans stretch a meal a long way. Stuff them in quesadillas, peppers or burgers and nobody leaves hungry.

benefits.title: Fiber
benefits.detail: A cup has about 15 grams, more than half of what most adults need in a day.

benefits.title: Plant protein
benefits.detail: About the same again in protein, which makes beans a cheap way to fill up.

benefits.title: Folate
benefits.detail: Beans are one of the richest everyday sources.

choose: Canned is easiest. Dried beans are even cheaper if you cook a big batch and freeze it.
store: Once opened, keep them covered in the fridge for 3–4 days, or freeze cooked beans in portions.
kidTip: Mash some into quesadillas. They hold everything together.

headline: Good fat, creamy everything
intro: Avocado makes toast, tacos and salads feel like a treat, and it's one of the few fruits that's mostly healthy fat.

benefits.title: Unsaturated fat
benefits.detail: Most of an avocado's fat is the monounsaturated kind, the same type as in olive oil.

benefits.title: Fiber
benefits.detail: A whole avocado has about 10 grams.

benefits.title: Potassium
benefits.detail: Avocados are a good source of this mineral.

choose: A ripe one gives slightly when you press it gently. Buy a couple of firm ones to ripen later in the week.
store: Ripen them on the counter, then keep ripe ones in the fridge for 2–3 more days. Wrap a cut half with the pit in and a little lemon juice.
kidTip: Mash onto toast with a pinch of salt. It's a whole snack.

headline: Protein in a tub
intro: Breakfast, sauces, marinades, dips: plain Greek yogurt does a lot of jobs, and it's thick enough to stand in for sour cream.

benefits.title: Protein
benefits.detail: Straining makes it about twice as high in protein as regular yogurt. ¾ cup has around 15 grams.

benefits.title: Calcium
benefits.detail: Like other dairy, it helps you get enough for strong bones.

benefits.title: Live cultures
benefits.detail: Look for "live and active cultures" on the label.

choose: Buy plain and sweeten it yourself. Flavored ones can have a lot of added sugar.
store: Keep it in the fridge and use it within about a week of opening.
kidTip: Set out a parfait bar with fruit and granola and let everyone build their own.

headline: Meaty flavor, hardly any calories
intro: Mushrooms bring deep, savory flavor. Chop them into ground meat to stretch it further, or let them be the star.

benefits.title: Very light
benefits.detail: A cup of sliced mushrooms has only about 15 calories.

benefits.title: B vitamins
benefits.detail: Mushrooms are a good source of riboflavin and niacin, which help your body use energy from food.

benefits.title: Stretch the meat
benefits.detail: Swapping half the ground meat for finely chopped mushrooms keeps the flavor and cuts saturated fat.

choose: Pick firm, dry mushrooms. Skip slimy or wrinkled ones.
store: Keep them in a paper bag in the fridge for up to a week, and don't wash them until you cook them.
kidTip: Chop them very finely into burgers or sauce. No one will spot them.

headline: Sturdy greens that last all week
intro: Unlike delicate lettuce, kale holds up in the fridge and in the pot, so it's still good on Friday.

benefits.title: Vitamins K and C
benefits.detail: Kale is one of the richest leafy greens for both.

benefits.title: Vitamin A
benefits.detail: Dark leafy greens are a good source of beta-carotene.

benefits.title: Fiber
benefits.detail: Kale's fiber helps soups and stews keep you full.

choose: Look for firm, deeply colored leaves. Baby kale is tender enough to eat raw.
store: Wrap it loosely and keep it in the fridge for up to a week. Chop and freeze extra for soups.
kidTip: Kale chips: tear it up, add a little oil and salt, and bake until crisp.

headline: The blank-canvas protein
intro: Tofu takes on whatever sauce you give it and crisps up beautifully. It's quick, cheap and keeps well.

benefits.title: Complete protein
benefits.detail: Soy has all the essential amino acids, like meat does.

benefits.title: Calcium
benefits.detail: Tofu set with calcium sulfate (check the ingredients) is a good source.

benefits.title: Low in saturated fat
benefits.detail: It's an easy swap in stir-fries and curries.

choose: Extra-firm is best for stir-fries and baking. Silken tofu is for soups and smoothies.
store: Once opened, cover it with water in a container, change the water daily, and use within 3–5 days. Freezing makes it chewier, which some people love.
kidTip: Cube it, toss it in cornstarch, and pan-fry until crisp. Think tofu nuggets.

headline: The fastest real meal there is
intro: Breakfast, lunch or a nothing-in-the-fridge dinner: eggs are protein that's ready in minutes.

benefits.title: High-quality protein
benefits.detail: Two eggs have about 12 grams, with all the essential amino acids.

benefits.title: Choline
benefits.detail: Yolks are one of the richest sources of this nutrient, which helps the brain and liver.

benefits.title: Vitamins D and B12
benefits.detail: Both are in the yolk, so eat the whole egg.

choose: Open the carton and check for cracks before you buy.
store: Keep them in their carton on a fridge shelf, not in the door, for 3–5 weeks.
kidTip: Egg bites or a cheesy scramble are easy wins.
